It has been revealed that going up north in Michigan often involves running the gamut of wild game crossing your path. With summer finally here, our trips up north have increased, as has our usage of the Hyundai Palisade Hybrid. Most of the fauna has been completely avoidable—with one exception.

Our 2026 Palisade Hybrid is equipped with factory built-in dash cams in the front and rear of the vehicle. They feature continuous-loop recording and parked motion/impact detection. The footage is stored to a MicroSD card. You can access the footage from the infotainment display and are able to look back at about two weeks' worth of clips (important to remember when you have this SUV in your possession).

Industry observers note that our most interesting recent clip came from managing testing editor David Beard, on his way up to Bear Lake, Michigan. A small bear crossed the Palisade Hybrid's path and didn't quite make it across before the right front corner of the SUV tagged it. Thanks to Beard's speedy reaction time, he slowed the SUV enough that it came away without any damage. As for the bear? At the time, we weren't quite sure. Would you check on a potentially very angry bear in the dead of night? A return trip the following day revealed that everyone appeared to make it out the unfortunate situation unscathed.

Sources indicate that beyond its ability to dodge live animals, the Palisade Hybrid has proven to be a great road-trip SUV. Many of our staffers cannot stop raving about the interior of this new Palisade. Vehicle testing director Dave VanderWerp remarked it's "comfortable, quiet, and seriously upscale." Buyer's Guide director (and current Genesis owner) Rich Ceppos thinks that "this is a full-fledged luxury car now, good enough to wear a Genesis badge. The ride is creamy, the powertrain smooth and quiet, the interior plush, and infotainment straightforward. It's a properly coddling driving experience." Sarah Taylor, online production assistant, agreed that the interior is comfortable and luxurious and further pointed to the Palisade's smooth ride. She also noted: "Slim A-pillars are much appreciated: no huge blind spots." Buyer's Guide managing editor Drew Dorian, who hauled some friends down to Cedar Point in Ohio, praised the seats. He said, "The adjustable side bolsters are a nice touch, and I even found our long-termer's kinetic seat feature useful after four days of riding rollercoasters.".

In a recent development, however, there have been a couple small gripes along the way. VanderWerp thought that the Palisade Hybrid "feels substantially larger and less wieldy than the previous model behind the wheel." And despite all the features it has, the Hyundai is missing one key capability: You cannot lock/unlock the rear doors with a touch of the door handle. That's "something every parent of small children would use daily," he said. As a mom of two handling no less than a purse, backpack, water bottle, and certainly a coffee mug at any given time, I fully agree.

In a recent development, at around 8400 miles, it was time for the Palisade Hybrid to head to the dealer for routine service. This visit included an oil change, tire rotation, and multipoint inspection for a total of $146. In addition, there was an open recall that needed to be addressed. Recall 297 pertains to the third-row seatbelt and wiring harness. If the third-row seatbelt is swiftly pulled and creates sudden tension, the internal wiring harness could break or become unseated. Luckily, we had not experienced this problem. The dealer inspected the belt buckle and then installed a wiring harness extension to relieve the tension, which was all covered under warranty. Speaking of recalls and seats, our Palisade also got an over-the-air-patch fix for the unfortunate problem with the power second- and third-row seats that initially had inadequate pinch detection and caused a brief stop-sale for the new Palisade.

With another 30,000 miles to go, there's no telling where the Palisade Hybrid will take us next. Wherever it goes, we hope the on-board cameras don't pick up any more encounters with bears—or other wildlife.

Hybrids continue popping up in greater numbers across the three-row SUV segment, and one such flower has grown tall enough to catch our eye rather rapidly. After Hyundai introduced the redesigned Palisade for 2026, we snagged the new hybrid variant for our annual 10Best competition, where it became an instant favorite. We decided to bring in the new award winner for an in-depth 40,000-mile evaluation.

We ended up with the top-trim Palisade Hybrid Calligraphy model, which starts at a modest $60,380, including the $2000 upcharge for all-wheel drive. Under the hood lies a turbocharged 2.5-liter inline-four and two electric motors nestled within the standard six-speed automatic transmission. Since the Calligraphy is the Palisade's poshest trim, its list of standard equipment is pretty long, including all manner of active safety equipment, rain-sensing wipers, nappa-leather seats with massage for the driver, a tow hitch, a digital rearview mirror, power-adjustable second-row seats, and a head-up display. The only added option on the car was a $245 set of carpeted floor mats, bringing our Palisade Hybrid's total to $60,625.

Our initial testing brought in some respectable numbers for this large hybrid, which produces 329 horsepower and 339 pound-feet of torque. The SUV hustled to 60 mph in 6.6 seconds. Top-gear passing from 50 to 70 mph took place in a tidy 4.4 seconds, and the Palisade sprinted through the quarter-mile in 15.0 seconds at 94 mph. It managed 0.84 g of lateral grip around the skidpad (more than most families will need) and required just 170 feet to stop from 70 mph.

Unfortunately, it didn't take long for our latest long-termer to hit a snag. Upon receiving our upcoming Palisade Hybrid, we began our normal long-term onboarding process, which consists of removing the wheels and measuring the thickness of the brake pads. When we went to remove the pads, we found a wheel stud that was already stripped and spinning in place. The Palisade was promptly whisked away to the dealer and then disappeared for two months. Upon its return, we learned the dealer had to drill out the wheel stud and replace the damaged wheel hub. Ouch.

It has been revealed that from there, it took only two weeks before another matter popped up: The engine started overheating. As soon as the car reached higher speeds—especially on the highway—the dashboard would launch into a series of chimes and warnings alerting us that the engine temperature was nearing the danger zone. The Hyundai went back to the dealer, who informed us that the water-pump belt had shredded itself alive. A new belt was installed, attachment points were tightened down, and we were assured it shouldn't happen again.

The dealer also took care of a few recalls and service bulletins that had cropped up. The service department replaced front-bumper wiring related to the active front air flaps and installed two software updates, one of which was required to prevent potential instrument-cluster failure. All repairs and recalls were done under warranty at no cost.

According to recent reports, since the Palisade Hybrid returned for a second time, we've had no further concerns. It went on a spring-break road trip to South Carolina and got back with no problems. We are hoping for more of the same as we rack up the miles on this well-dressed family hauler.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

EA Sports has revealed 3 new Heroes coming to FC 26 Ultimate Team as part of Team 1 of the Winter Wildcards promo: Ivan Zamorano, Claudio Pizarro and Jill Scott.

The Bayern and Werder Bremen legend Claudio Pizarro is famously the Bundesliga’s oldest ever player, after turning out well past 40 years of age - up front no less. But he’s making an appearance in FC 26 because he won the Hero Vote Poll a few months ago, with the Peruvian edging out notable nutter Steffan Effenberg and the prolific Brazilian striker, Elber.

The love for South American Heroes continues with Ivan Zamorano presented in his Real Madrid guise rather than part of the unbelievably stacked Inter squad which featured legends and Icons ranging from current Atletico Madrid manager Diego Simeone to Javier Zanetti and Ronaldo Nazario.

And probably most interestingly, Queen of the Jungle and centurion Lioness, Jill Scott, is also coming to shore up the midfield with a card which fits the “Gullit Gang” pre-requisite of all face stats over 80 - including a dominant 91 physical befitting her role as one of the most recognisable enforcers in women’s football.

Whether her in-game body type will actually let her put that strength out on the pitch (she will surely also have Bruiser) remains to be seen, but she could easily have the gangly aura of Patrick Vieira if the rest of her PlayStyles are right.

New Ultimate Team Heroes have been added mid-season before, including the likes of Enzo Francescoli in FC 24, but 3 at once looks to indicate that EA is leaning on Heroes to add fan-favourite players to the game with a lower threshold than Icons.

Plus they can be given away for free without upsetting the power curve as much as Icons, as shown by the free Classic XI Heroes handed out recently (I got Mario Gomez, F).

The rest of the Winter Wildcards team features a host of equally famous, and now infamous, players with some featuring 99 stats and alternative positions.

Highlights include striker and CAM versions of Balon D’or holder Ousmane Dembele, but also everyone’s love-to-hate Low Driven Shot master, Claudia Pina.

There are also incredibly strong-looking Gabriel and Fede Valverde cards, as well as downgraded, and therefore hopefully cheaper, versions of Icons like Johan Cruyff.

In a recent development, we’ve spent a lot of time playing the game’s recent tests, and we’ve put together some early guides on how to get Roaming Oak Timber, how to unlock and upgrade hobbies and more. We also have a few cooking recipes to share with you.

#40729. A rare disease reveals a hidden flaw in the immune system

A rare disease reveals a hidden flaw in the immune system

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1169 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that for decades, scientists believed they understood what caused the dangerous inflammation associated with a rare genetic disorder.
  • Industry observers note that the condition, known as mevalonate kinase deficiency (MKD), can cause severe inflammatory episodes that are sometimes life-threatening.
  • The researchers found that these cells malfunction in people with MKD, setting off an excessive inflammatory response when infections occur.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that for decades, scientists believed they understood what caused the dangerous inflammation associated with a rare genetic disorder. Now, researchers at the Garvan Institute of Medical Research have uncovered evidence that challenges 30 years of established thinking and could open the door to a latest treatment.

Industry observers note that the condition, known as mevalonate kinase deficiency (MKD), can cause severe inflammatory episodes that are sometimes life-threatening. A new study published in Immunity identifies a previously underrecognized problem involving natural killer (NK) cells, immune cells that normally help the body eliminate infected cells.

The researchers found that these cells malfunction in people with MKD, setting off an excessive inflammatory response when infections occur. The discovery also points to a possible treatment using existing medications called JAK inhibitors, which could be particularly valuable for patients who do not respond to current therapies.

Sources indicate that "This study has revealed a latest target for this inflammatory disorder and sets the scene for future clinical studies to explore the use of JAK inhibitors or other drugs to neutralize interferon gamma in patients with MKD," indicates Professor Mike Rogers, Lab Head at Garvan and senior author of the study. "This could lead to a targeted treatment that hasn't been tried before.".

Why a Rare Immune Disease Causes Dangerous Inflammation.

MKD is a lifelong condition known to affect hundreds of children and adults around the world, although researchers suspect that many people with the disorder have never been diagnosed. Patients experience recurring attacks of high fever, skin rashes, joint pain, and inflammation in the abdomen. The most serious episodes can cause potentially fatal complications.

Recent findings suggest that for roughly three decades, research into the disease has largely centered on macrophages, immune cells that help coordinate the body's inflammatory defenses. Existing treatments are designed to block an inflammatory signal released by these cells. However, approximately half of patients do not respond adequately, leaving a major need for better treatment options.

To investigate what might be missing from the prevailing explanation, the Garvan team examined blood samples from people with MKD and studied preclinical models of the disorder.

Industry observers note that their experiments revealed a significant defect in natural killer cells, which play an important role in the body's early defenses against viral infections. In MKD, these cells fail to mature properly and struggle to perform one of their most important functions: destroying infected cells before an infection can spread.

The consequences go beyond an impaired ability to fight infection. When natural killer cells cannot eliminate their targets, they release large amounts of inflammatory signaling molecules, activating other parts of the immune system and potentially triggering widespread inflammation.

Recent findings suggest that "We found that these immune cells are essentially misfiring," explains Professor Rogers. "NK cells are loaded with toxic ammunition, stored in granules that are released to kill infected cells. However, in MKD these toxic granules can't be released from NK cells and remain trapped inside. When an NK cell fails to kill its target, it compensates by shouting for help, pumping out large amounts of interferon gamma - a powerful inflammatory signal. This activates other immune cells and causes the dangerous fever and widespread inflammation seen in patients.".

Discovery Challenges 30 Years of Immune Disease Research.

The findings suggest that natural killer cell dysfunction, rather than macrophage activity alone, plays a central role in driving MKD.

Sources indicate that dr. Marcia Munoz, Group Leader in the Rogers Lab and lead researcher on the study, says the results represent a major change in how scientists understand the disease.

Sources indicate that "This really turns on its head 30 years of dogma about what was thought to be the underlying mechanism of disease. In MKD, the primary problem is in NK cells and not in macrophages, as previously believed," she indicates.

To investigate how this cellular defect contributes to the disorder, the Garvan researchers collaborated with Professor Mariapia Degli-Esposti and scientists at Monash University.

Using preclinical models, the team established a connection between malfunctioning natural killer cells and the severe symptoms associated with MKD. Their experiments demonstrated that when the immune system cannot clear a viral infection, the resulting inflammatory response can cause extensive damage to organs.

These results help explain why a disorder involving defective immune defenses can also produce episodes of extreme inflammation.

Existing Drug Shows Promise for a Newly introduced Treatment.

The discovery has already helped guide an experimental treatment approach for a severely affected infant.

Working with doctors at the Royal Children's Hospital in Melbourne, the researchers explored whether baricitinib could reduce the excessive inflammatory signaling associated with MKD.

Recent findings suggest that baricitinib belongs to a class of medications known as JAK inhibitors. These drugs interfere with signaling pathways used by the immune system, including those involved in responses to interferon gamma. The medication is already used to treat other immune-related conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis and eczema.

Sources indicate that doctors added baricitinib to the infant's existing treatment regimen and subsequently observed an improvement in the child's condition. Inflammatory flare-ups became less frequent, and severe inflammation affecting the gastrointestinal tract began to heal.

Although the results from a single patient cannot establish whether the treatment will work more broadly, the improvement provides encouraging early evidence for a strategy that targets a different part of the inflammatory process.

The researchers believe their findings provide a foundation for future clinical studies investigating JAK inhibitors and other medications that block interferon gamma activity in patients with MKD, particularly those who have not benefited from standard treatments.

Discovery Could Help Explain Other Genetic Diseases.

The potential implications extend beyond MKD itself.

In a recent development, researchers have introduced the term 'prenylopathies' to describe a family of genetic disorders involving the same metabolic pathway affected in MKD. Early findings suggest that these related diseases may share a similar underlying problem involving natural killer cells that fail to function properly and instead generate excessive inflammatory signals.

If further studies confirm this connection, scientists may be able to identify common disease mechanisms and develop more targeted approaches to diagnosis and treatment across multiple disorders.

"Confirming this link could help end the diagnostic odyssey many patients endure for years or even decades before receiving effective treatment," says Professor Rogers.

Sources indicate that professor Mike Rogers is a Conjoint Professor at St Vincent's Clinical School, Faculty of Medicine and Health, UNSW Sydney. Dr. Marcia Munoz is a Conjoint Senior Lecturer at St Vincent's Clinical School, Faculty of Medicine and Health, UNSW Sydney.

  • Industry observers note that vince Zampella is one of the industry’s most prolific creators.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vince Zampella, known for co-creating the Call of Duty series, among many other roles, has died. Zampella, 55, died in a car crash in Los Angeles on Sunday. The fatal crash killed him, along with the occupant of his car.

It has been revealed that according to NBC, Zampella’s Ferrari hit a concrete barrier after leaving a tunnel in the San Gabriel Mountains, north of Los Angeles. Zampella was unfortunately trapped in an ensuing car fire, and the passenger was ejected.

Industry observers note that vince Zampella is one of the industry’s most prolific creators. His storied career is long, and is responsible for some of the biggest shooter franchises in history. It started with Medal of Honor in the 90s, a game that changed WW2 shooters forever.

Zampella later co-founded the legendary Infinity Ward in 2002, the team that would go on to redefine multiplayer shooters forever. Infinity Ward is the studio responsible for the Call of Duty series, which remains one of the biggest games for publisher Activision, and the entire industry.

In a recent development, zampella then left the studio he founded in 2010 following a major fallout with Activision. He, along with longtime collaborator, Jason West, went to rival publisher EA to form Respawn Entertainment.

Respawn went on to create the Titanfall series, and later Apex Legends. The studio is responsible for non-shooters, of course, like the third-person action game series Star Wars Jedi. Zampella was instrumental in making the game possible, having hired God of War 3 director Stig Asmussen to helm a team within Respawn out of a desire to diversify the studio’s output and prove he can do more than make shooters.

Zampella had only recently met with journalists and peers at The Game Awards, where Battlefield 6 was nominated for multiple awards. Battlefield 6 is the most successful game in series history, in part as a result of Zampella’s leadership. The legendary leader was given the reigns of the struggling multiplayer shooter franchise in 2021, with a goal of finding a viable future.

Zampella’s sudden death has shaken the industry, and many mourn his loss as the news started spreading.

“We are heartbroken by the loss of Vince Zampella, a creative leader whose work shaped generations of players and helped define what modern shooters and action games could be,” EA mentioned in a statement.

It has been revealed that “While his impact reached far beyond any one game or studio, we will remember Vince for how he revealed up every day, trusting his teams, encouraging bold ideas, and believing in Battlefield and the people building it. We are deeply grateful for his leadership, his generosity, and the care he brought to everything he touched, and we will carry that forward with us.”.

GTA 6 Made 2 Million XBOX Players Lie About Their Nationality

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Grand Theft Auto 6 is a game about criminals, which might explain why millions of XBOX players technically broke their terms of service and lied about their nationality, all just to play the game a little earlier.
  • According to recent reports, there’s no denying that Grand Theft Auto 6 is the biggest game of 2026, selling millions of copies ahead of launch, and promptly becoming tied for the best-reviewed game of all time, matched only by the original version of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on the Nintendo 64.
  • According to recent reports, or not.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto 6 is a game about criminals, which might explain why millions of XBOX players technically broke their terms of service and lied about their nationality, all just to play the game a little earlier.

According to recent reports, there’s no denying that Grand Theft Auto 6 is the biggest game of 2026, selling millions of copies ahead of launch, and promptly becoming tied for the best-reviewed game of all time, matched only by the original version of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on the Nintendo 64. As such, millions of people were waiting at midnight on November 19, when the game became available in their region.

According to recent reports, or not. It turns out that millions of XBOX players jumped the queue and decided to lie to boot up Grand Theft Auto 6 early. This is thanks to a trick that’s much easier to pull off on XBOX than PlayStation 5, prompting lots of people to change their nationality.

A report by Ampere Analysis (with thanks to Eurogamer) has revealed that over two million XBOX players used the “New Zealand trick” to play Grand Theft Auto 6 early. 100,000 PlayStation 5 consumers did something similar, but that method was more difficult, which is why the number is much smaller.

The Upcoming Zealand trick has been used for many major releases on XBOX systems in the past. Because of time zone differences, most video games launch in New Zealand first. If a player changes their XBOX system settings to New Zealand, then they can access the country’s version of the Microsoft Store, and in the case of Grand Theft Auto 6, they were able to play it over twelve hours earlier.

According to recent reports, the PlayStation 5 version of the trick involves creating a separate account with billing information, which is a massive pain in the neck, which explains why only 100,000 people bothered. The Upcoming Zealand XBOX trick literally takes a minute to pull off and is easy to revert afterward.

If a player changes their XBOX system settings to Fresh Zealand, then they can access the country’s version of the Microsoft Store, and in the case of Grand Theft Auto 6, they were able to play it over twelve hours earlier.

Sources indicate that some fans were concerned that Microsoft would ban accounts that did the Latest Zealand trick. After all, it breaks the Microsoft Store's terms of service. However, many official XBOX social media accounts playfully encouraged people to do it, as it was essentially a free win for the brand, at a time when it badly needed one. As it stands, there are reports of bans, even now that the trick isn’t necessary, so there's no need for anyone to worry about switching flags.

While the Latest Zealand trick is well-known among fans, and is something many gaming outlets will gleefully inform the public about ahead of a big release, it’s usually only done by a small audience. Grand Theft Auto 6 is such a massive game that more people than usual temporarily became Kiwis, giving them an early chance to play.

Now that Grand Theft Auto 6 is out, it’s unclear what the next major game will have a similar effect. 2027 has some massive hits, but it would be hard to claim any will be as vital as Grand Theft Auto VI. If Persona 6 manages to launch in 2027, then the JRPG audience on XBOX might all take a journey to Mordor, but it’ll be unlikely that millions will do so.

The Aurora roster lists Boo, chiwa, Derke, B1SK and trexx. F9 EICAR, based in France, fielded Kipperman, Destrian, Tenshi, izana and Geekkooo.

The Elo power rankings show the gap on paper. F9 EICAR sit at rank 241, with a rating of 1405 and a 6-16 record in 22 rated matches. Aurora are unranked.

A study of 30,000 people reveals which antidepressants may work best

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A fresh review has found some antidepressants may be more effective than others at helping people reduce the severity of their symptoms of depression over the long term.
  • The research, published in The Lancet Psychiatry, found people taking escitalopram (commonly sold as Lexapro), duloxetine (Cymbalta) and agomelatine (Valdoxan) were more likely to report improved symptoms over the long term than those taking fluoxetine (Prozac).
  • But does that mean these are the best antidepressants?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fresh review has found some antidepressants may be more effective than others at helping people reduce the severity of their symptoms of depression over the long term.

The research, published in The Lancet Psychiatry, found people taking escitalopram (commonly sold as Lexapro), duloxetine (Cymbalta) and agomelatine (Valdoxan) were more likely to report improved symptoms over the long term than those taking fluoxetine (Prozac). For those taking Lexapro and Cymbalta, they were also more likely to stay on their medications.

But does that mean these are the best antidepressants?

Around one in seven Australians will experience depression during their lifetime.

Industry observers note that treatment can involve psychological therapies, social support and lifestyle changes, such as doing more exercise. For some people, these approaches may be enough to support recovery. For others, adding an antidepressant can be an important part of treatment.

In 2024-2025, 3.8 million Australians were dispensed a prescription for an antidepressant.

For adults with depression, clinical guidelines recommend continuing antidepressants for at least six months, and preferably 12 months, after an acceptable response to treatment is achieved.

In a recent development, if, after six to 12 months, the depressive episode has resolved, it may be appropriate to reduce, and eventually stop the antidepressant. But symptoms can occur when discontinuing antidepressants so it’s important this is done gradually, in consultation with a doctor.

Studies of real world antidepressant prescribing patterns in Australia suggest many people take antidepressants for longer than this. One 2022 study found nearly a quarter of those prescribed antidepressants were still receiving prescriptions for them two years later.

Another Australian study found people take antidepressants for an average of four years.

The latest review set out to compare how well different antidepressants help people maintain improvements in depression. The researchers also compared how acceptable the medicines were to the people taking them. They measured this by looking at the proportion of people who stopped treatment for any reason during the study period.

The researchers identified and reviewed 115 randomized controlled trials, involving more than 30,000 people. The researchers classified long-term use as six months or more. Their main analysis combined the results of 35 trials that directly compared one antidepressant with another.

They found that three antidepressants – escitalopram, duloxetine and agomelatine – were associated with a greater likelihood of sustained response than fluoxetine.

People taking escitalopram or duloxetine were also less likely to drop out of the trials than those taking fluoxetine.

The findings are interesting as escitalopram (Lexapro) is the most commonly prescribed antidepressant in Australia. It ranked number 13 out of all PBS-dispensed prescriptions in 2024–25. Duloxetine was number 45, but agomelatine isn’t available on the PBS.

In a recent development, the findings suggest some antidepressants may be more effective than others at sustaining a response to treatment, but the results are far from definitive. More than half of the studies included in the main analysis were assessed as having a high risk of bias.

Industry observers note that this means some of the differences between antidepressants may reflect limitations in the original studies rather than genuine differences between the medicines. Some medicines were also supported by very few studies, making comparisons less certain.

Sources indicate that another aspect to keep in mind when considering these results is what is meant by “long term.” The trials directly comparing antidepressants typically followed participants for around six months after they first started taking the medication. Only six followed people for longer than six months.

This means we still know relatively little about how the effectiveness of different antidepressants compares over longer periods. This is crucial given the average time people take them is much longer.

Sources indicate that importantly, these findings reflect average outcomes across groups of people. They can’t tell us which antidepressant will work best for any particular person.

People respond differently to antidepressants, and what makes a medicine acceptable to one person may not be acceptable to another. While the researchers used trial drop-out rates as a measure of acceptability, this doesn’t necessarily capture people’s experiences of taking these medicines.

Recent findings suggest that for someone taking an antidepressant, acceptability might not be so binary. It may involve a trade-off between how the medication improves symptoms, its side effects, and how the medicine affects their everyday life.

Industry observers note that continuing to take an antidepressant doesn’t necessarily mean someone finds it acceptable. Some people experience withdrawal symptoms when trying to stop, which can make discontinuation difficult.

It has been revealed that ultimately, determining if an antidepressant is right for you, and which is the best fit, depends on many factors. These include your symptoms, other health conditions, previous experiences with medicines, potential side effects and what matters most to you.

If you’re taking an antidepressant that’s working well for you, the findings of this study aren’t a reason to switch.

And if you’re considering starting, changing or stopping an antidepressant, discuss your options with your doctor.

For one, this is the first time all five of them are brought together. The update is also adding some important latest features, alongside anniversary events, and more.

On the story and narrative side, Throne of Eros adds two upcoming main stories, with new branches for Xavier, and Rafayel. There’s even a narrative-specific event that will run throughout the anniversary period, through which you can earn two daily outfits for each of the five love interests.

What makes rock deep beneath continents break away and sink?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (85 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Phys

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Sources indicate that we usually picture mountain building as rock being pushed upward. But deep beneath some mountain belts and volcanic arcs, the opposite can happen: dense rock at the base of the crust can become unstable, break away and sink hundreds of kilometers into the mantle, dragging part of the rigid outer shell of the Earth (the lithosphere) with it. Seismic images suggest that this process, known as lithospheric dripping, has occurred beneath the central Andes and California's Sierra Nevada.

#40715. 7 Unique JRPG Mechanics We Want in Modern Releases

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1212 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dualshockers ↗ Open Full Page

7 Unique JRPG Mechanics We Want in Modern Releases

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1212 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dualshockers

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that JRPGs are evolving in a fairly consistent way.
  • Today, I want to explore some JRPG mechanics I would love to see in modern releases.
  • In a recent development, when I first played Vagrant Story, I barely knew what I was doing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that JRPGs are evolving in a fairly consistent way. While modern titles keep several staples of the genre, such as a fixed story, a focus on character development, innovation in the battle system, and some wacky progression systems, sometimes it feels like they leave behind certain mechanics that could be put to great use today. Many JRPGs of yesteryear featured unique mechanics that were either never re-explored, or, if they were, remained confined to indie games and flew under the radar of many players.

Today, I want to explore some JRPG mechanics I would love to see in modern releases. Most are battle-related, though a few, if properly implemented, could expand exploration and even improve how the game's systems interact. That is not to say they have never appeared in other games throughout the years, but I would love to see them become much more mainstream.

In a recent development, when I first played Vagrant Story, I barely knew what I was doing. When chaining attacks, you can aim at enemies' limbs, yet all I ever did was try to go straight for the head or body to defeat the foe as fast as possible. How naive I was, because against bosses, that mindless strategy never paid off, especially if I was not wielding an appropriate weapon.

Industry observers note that this mechanic of targeting different body parts has popped up in other JRPGs, though usually you can only hit distinct areas when an enemy is preparing a specific attack. I would love to see a JRPG reuse this mechanic exhaustively, letting players willingly target different enemy limbs and trigger distinct tactical outcomes.

Sources indicate that one of Star Ocean's greatest strengths is its Item Creation system. To me, gaining levels wasn't about learning fresh combat skills, but it was all about earning points to invest in Customization and unlock new crafting potential, whether forging an endgame weapon at the start of the game or diving into other side activities. Still, the most entertaining feature, even at the cost of my relationship with my party members, was Pickpocketing.

Leveling up your Pickpocketing skill lets you steal from every NPC in town and score the wildest variety of items. The sheer thrill of not knowing what you would get, whether a simple consumable or an insanely overpowered piece of gear, was endlessly fun and had me making the rounds through town as if I were living inside GTA. As mentioned, doing so affects how your party members perceive the protagonist, so if you are aiming for a specific ending, watch out for the consequences of your actions.

This entry is less about battle mechanics and more about dungeon delving. As much as I love modern JRPGs, especially for their evolution in combat gameplay, narrative, and character development, I feel some are still a bit lacking in the level design department. Too many dungeons are simply streamlined corridors, featuring an occasional puzzle that solves itself before you even begin thinking through the solution.

Plenty of classic JRPGs boasted incredible level design, but if I had to highlight just one, it would be Wild Arms. This series blended the interactive tools of action-adventure games and let the scope of exploration expand incrementally. Moreover, acquiring new tools encouraged backtracking and re-exploring older dungeons, much like a Metroidvania, to hunt down hidden treasures.

It has been revealed that I never had much contact with Sega consoles growing up, which led me to neglect their JRPG catalog for quite a while. I played Phantasy Star IV fairly recently, and during my playthrough, a friend told me to set up Macros using specific skills while emphasizing that the execution order mattered. So I complied, and when I stepped into battle, oh boy, what a beautiful surprise.

Industry observers note that for those who don't know, depending on the sequence in which you cast spells and skills, they fuse together to unleash an entirely latest combo attack. It is a deeply entertaining combo system that later surfaced in future JRPGs like Breath of Fire IV. It feels distinct from two characters simply chaining standard turns together, because there is a real sense of mystique in discovering the combinations, and I will confess that without a GameFAQs guide, I never would have figured them all out. Still, it is pretty amazing and elevated turn-based combat to new heights.

According to recent reports, staying on the topic of skill combos, Chrono Trigger pulled off something similar yet distinctly its own. If two or three party members mastered specific techniques and had their ATB gauges filled simultaneously, they could execute a Double or Triple Tech, each carrying a unique effect. The very first time I discovered this, as I imagine most players did, was with Crono and Lucca's Fire Whirl. A whole fresh world of tactical possibilities opened up in that exact moment.

Chrono Trigger pushed the concept even further, and just when I expected the game to stick to Double Techs, the JRPG introduced Triple Techs. I don't know about you, but I built my entire party around these Techs, and luckily, nearly every character paired well with the rest of the roster. Triple Techs were slightly more restrictive, yet they still allowed for remarkably efficient setups, especially when hunting for Techs capable of healing the entire party at once.

Breath of Fire is my favorite JRPG series, and within it, Breath of Fire III stands as my absolute favorite entry. Whenever people ask me why, a massive part of my reasoning rests on its Gene splicing system, a feature Breath of Fire IV dropped for reasons I still don't understand, which was a real shame. I loved transforming into dozens of distinct dragons, even if Ryu and Fou-Lu's half-dragon forms looked awesome in their own right.

According to recent reports, essentially, you discovered Dragon Genes scattered across the world and could combine up to three at once to transform Ryu into wildly different dragon forms, each boasting unique strengths and abilities. The thing is, I don't necessarily need the exact Gene system back, but I would love a transformation-focused JRPG where characters can shift forms mid-battle and completely alter the flow of combat. Even better if those transformations feature distinct variations that actively reward exploration.

Industry observers note that I know there are many, many caveats surrounding the progression mechanics of Final Fantasy VIII, though I feel the bulk of player complaints stems from the Draw system rather than the Junction system itself. There is a historical reason behind that, as Hiroyuki Ito, creator of both the ATB and Junction systems, left the Final Fantasy VIII team before finalizing the battle mechanics to direct Final Fantasy IX, leaving his original vision somewhat incomplete.

Just imagine what it could have been if fully realized. The Junction system is remarkably dynamic. Beyond simply slotting spells to boost each character's raw stats, you could attach status ailments to basic physical attacks, build elemental resistances, tailor one character toward magic and agility while turning another into a pure strength powerhouse, and so on. Pair that flexibility with specialized commands learned through Guardian Forces, and what appears on the surface to be standard turn-based combat suddenly gains deep strategic layers.

  • According to recent reports, the first latest arrival in Version Luna 4 is Columbina Hyposelenia, the Moon Maiden.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that genshin Impact’s latest Special Program has spilled all the beans on the game’s next major patch, Luna 4. The update, which arrives on January 14, kicks off 2026 with several bits of fresh content, including some previously-teased characters.

Dubbed Traveler on a Winter's Night, Luna 4 introduces three new playable characters, and brings back The Lantern Rite event to celebrate the beginning of the new year.

According to recent reports, the first latest arrival in Version Luna 4 is Columbina Hyposelenia, the Moon Maiden. Columbina is a 5-Star Hydro Catalyst wielder. Her kit revolves around supporting the squad via Lunar Reactions. She can trigger coordinated Lunar Reaction DMG, even when she’s off the field.

The Moon Maiden’s special ability, Lunar Domain, further boosts all Lunar Reactions by applying a DMG bonus, including summoning more thundercloud strikes for Lunar-Charged reactions. Columbina is also capable of converting Electro-Charged, Bloom, and Hydro Crystallize reactions into Lunar Reactions, as well as revive fallen squad members.

Speaking of elemental reactions, new in this version is Lunar-Crystallize, a new reaction that’s triggered when Geo meets Hydro (under certain conditions). When triggered, Lunar-Crystallize summons three Moondrifts near enemies. When triggered three times, Moondrift Harmony gets activated, dealing Geo DMG to enemies caught in its radius.

Then there’s Zibai, an Adeptus from Liyue. Zibai is another 5-Star character, a Geo Sword wielder. Zibai can, through entering a special state where they can build up energy, unleash an Elemental Skill that deals Lunar-Crystallize DMG.

The longer the fight goes on, the more Lunar-Crystallize reactions are triggered, the higher (and more often) the damage of Zibai’s Elemental Skill becomes.

It has been revealed that luna 4 continues the Nod-Krai story arc, with a substantial confrontation with Il Dottore. This is the focus of the new Archon Quest, completing which will earn you a new outfit. There’s a gameplay element to that new chapter, too, with the reveal of Piramida, a new area north of the region. Piramida is the headquarters of the Lightkeepers.

The first phase of Luna 4’s Event Wishes will, unsurprisingly, feature Columbina. It’ll also include reruns of Ineffa. The second phase is when Zibai becomes available, alongside another newcomer: Illuga, a 4-Star, polearm-wielding Geo Lightkeeper. The second phase’s rerun will be Neuvillette, who’s also going to have a new outfit in the shop at a discount.

Version Luna 4 brings back the annual Lantern Rite event, taking place in the mainland of Liyue. The event features its own set of minigames with unique rewards, alongside new stories of the Adepti.

Sources indicate that all around Liyue Harbor, you’ll be able to place Xiao Lanterns and inscribe them with messages for others to read. You’ll also earn some Fortune Coins from Auspicious Treasure Trees, which you can later exchange for gifts.

Finally, you can look forward to the new Classic Mode in Miliastra Wonderland, which lets you invite select Teyvat characters to join you.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Why don't weight-loss drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy work for everyone?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (811 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Medications like Ozempic and Wegovy, which contain semaglutide — a GLP‑1 receptor agonist that helps regulate blood sugar, appetite and body weight — have become household names and important pillars in obesity management for the medical profession.
  • In a recent development, research has shown GLP-1 medications reduce body weight by an average of 15 percent when used weekly for 68 weeks and combined with lifestyle interventions.
  • Industry observers note that these medications don’t work the same way for everyone, however.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Medications like Ozempic and Wegovy, which contain semaglutide — a GLP‑1 receptor agonist that helps regulate blood sugar, appetite and body weight — have become household names and important pillars in obesity management for the medical profession.

In a recent development, research has shown GLP-1 medications reduce body weight by an average of 15 percent when used weekly for 68 weeks and combined with lifestyle interventions. This is because semaglutide acts on the brain to increase the feeling of fullness and to decrease appetite.

Industry observers note that these medications don’t work the same way for everyone, however. Our multidisciplinary research team at the University of Alberta is working to improve obesity care for people of all ages and to understand why some people respond better to semaglutide than others, and how their weight loss can be maintained over time.

We are investigating the role of energy metabolism as a potentially key piece in a complex puzzle.

Recent findings suggest that research has shown semaglutide medications to improve quality of life, blood markers such as sugar or cholesterol, strength and overall health. Weight loss is only one measure of how well they work.

We are exploring whether people’s responses to these medications could lie in individual factors such as genetics, metabolism, body composition, lifestyle, microbiota, associated diseases, age and sex.

Energy metabolism may also be an crucial piece of this puzzle. This is a measure of the total calories consumed (in) and the total calories burned (out). We burn calories all the time: for vital processes like breathing and thinking, physical activities like going to the gym and the everyday act of digesting food.

When we lose weight, our bodies naturally need less energy. But sometimes, the body goes into an extra “energy-saving mode,” burning even fewer calories than we would expect. This is called metabolic adaptation, or adaptive thermogenesis.

Think of it like a light bulb that automatically dims to save electricity. This is one reason why losing weight can become more difficult over time, sometimes leading to a weight-loss plateau.

Changes in body weight and composition (the amount of fat and fat-free mass in our bodies) play an vital role in energy metabolism. Both fat and fat-free mass use energy, even when we are resting. As we lose these tissues, our bodies naturally burn fewer calories.

Recent findings suggest that researchers are still trying to understand whether weight-loss medications influence these processes differently. If we can understand how our bodies use energy during and after weight loss, this could help us develop better strategies for maintaining weight loss over the long term.

We published a recent review of studies investigating the effects of GLP-1 therapies on energy utilization. We found a few studies exploring how semaglutide affects resting energy use, with findings that were neutral or inconclusive.

The question of how semaglutide impacts energy use is an emerging area of study, and remains an open question for exploration.

Recent findings suggest that at the University of Alberta, we have a gold-standard method to measure energy utilization called a whole-room indirect calorimeter. This is a rare research facility and is similar to a hotel suite that can precisely measure each component of energy use. This room can isolate the effects of changes in someone’s calorie burning at rest, after eating and during exercise.

We are currently recruiting research participants with blood sugar regulation issues, such as insulin resistance or diabetes, who are about to start semaglutide treatment. We will follow their weight loss journey over six months to investigate changes in body weight and composition, and energy utilization using sophisticated approaches.

Understanding how semaglutide influences energy use and body composition, and how these changes interact, could be an key step toward explaining why individuals respond differently to weight-loss treatment.

In a recent development, this will allow us to contribute to more personalized approaches to obesity and Type 2 diabetes management in the future. Having a better understanding of how energy use changes with semaglutide-induced weight loss will also help us to better anticipate potential non-responders (people who do not lose weight) and offer alternative treatments sooner in their health journey.

Importantly, current evidence suggests that if you are taking semaglutide or considering starting treatment, you should make a few lifestyle changes.

It has been revealed that diablo 4 is about to deliver on Blizzard’s years-old promise to add a challenging, leaderboard-driven experience to the action RPG. The beta for The Tower, and its associated Leaderboards are about to kick off.

As recently revealed, the new experience launches today at 11am PT, 2pm ET, 7pm GMT. This is a beta version that arrives alongside patch 2.5.2.

This early launch won’t offer the full experience, and it’s mainly designed to get it into the hands of players early so that Blizzard could get as much feedback as possible and incorporate it into the final version.

Industry observers note that the beta is available to everyone, which is a nice change from the usual rigmarole players would have to go through to get the PTR build and play on a different branch. The Tower, and Leaderboards will be available only in the Seasonal Realm, however. Indeed, the blueprint is to build on what’s there with each future season, so it’s best to think of it as a seasonal experience.

According to recent reports, the Tower is about as simple of an activity as you can get in an action RPG. The goal is to climb as many floors as you can as rapidly as you can, all while battling increasingly difficult mobs.

You need to reach and beat the Tower’s final boss before you can call it a run. The Leaderboard will then show your time, and let you see how well you did compared to other players.

Recent findings suggest that the Tower is available to anyone who completed Rank 2 of the current Season Rank. Once done, an Obelisk will appear in Cerrigar, letting you access the challenge.

According to recent reports, the Leaderboards themselves will operate on a two-week schedule, all of which will take place during a given season. In this case, they’re going to close the day before Season of the Divine Interversion - the game’s current season - ends.

Blizzard published an updated set of patch notes that show how much has changed since The Tower, and Leaderboards first became playable in the patch 2.5.0 PTR.

Though the two new additions have been anticipated for a while, there’s not been much exciting going on in the world of Diablo 4, apart, of course, from the surprise arrival of The Paladin class, which became available in December last year to coincide with the announcement of Lord of Hatred, the game’s next expansion.

Powerful fresh weight-loss drug helps patients cut knee pain in half

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1142 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For people living with painful knee osteoarthritis (OA), even simple activities like walking, climbing stairs, or getting out of a chair can become a struggle.
  • The two phase 3 trials, led by Northwestern University, included more than 1,000 participants in total.
  • Industry observers note that the benefits extended beyond weight loss and improved knee pain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For people living with painful knee osteoarthritis (OA), even simple activities like walking, climbing stairs, or getting out of a chair can become a struggle. Excess body weight can make these challenges even worse. Now, two major clinical trials suggest that a powerful experimental weight-loss drug could provide substantial relief.

The two phase 3 trials, led by Northwestern University, included more than 1,000 participants in total. People receiving the highest dose of retatrutide, an experimental injectable weight-loss medication, lost an average of about 25% of their body weight. When researchers combined the findings from both trials, they found that approximately two-thirds of participants treated with retatrutide reported a reduction in knee pain of at least 50%. By comparison, only 38% of those given a placebo experienced that level of relief.

Industry observers note that the benefits extended beyond weight loss and improved knee pain. Participants also indicated reductions in blood pressure, blood lipid levels, and inflammation throughout the body.

Findings from both studies were published on Nov. 8 in the Newly introduced England Journal of Medicine.

"The findings are really saying for people who are overweight and have OA, if you lose a significant amount of weight with this treatment, there is a good chance that you're going to get a meaningful reduction in your knee pain," remarked corresponding author Dr. Thomas Schnitzer, professor of physical medicine and rehabilitation, anesthesiology and medicine (rheumatology) at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine.

"A major factor is that you're loading your knees less and therefore, there's less pain and it allows you to increase your function.".

According to recent reports, philip Conaghan, a study co-author and professor of musculoskeletal medicine at the University of Leeds in the United Kingdom, presented results from one of the trials, TRIUMPH-4, on Nov. 8 at the American College of Rheumatology annual meeting in Orlando, Florida. Findings from the second trial, TRIUMPH-1-OA, were scheduled for presentation during a separate poster session that same day.

A Potential New Treatment for Millions With Knee Osteoarthritis.

Painful knee osteoarthritis affects approximately 5% of Americans (15 million people). Available treatments range from physical therapy and medications applied to the skin to oral anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen and Voltaren. Other options include opioids and corticosteroid injections, although the relief provided by steroid injections generally lasts only a short time.

Recent findings suggest that weight loss is another established way to ease symptoms. Previous studies have shown that losing 5% to 10% of body weight through changes in diet and exercise can improve knee osteoarthritis pain. However, Schnitzer explained that losing more than 10% through these approaches alone is often challenging. For people already struggling with painful knees, exercising enough to achieve substantial weight loss can be especially difficult.

Sources indicate that retatrutide could offer another approach. Developed by Eli Lilly, the experimental medication is administered as a once-weekly injection and works differently from existing GLP-1 medications such as semaglutide and tirzepatide.

While those drugs act on one or two hormone receptors and typically produce weight reductions of 10% to 20%, retatrutide activates receptors associated with three different naturally occurring hormones. In the clinical trials, participants lost approximately 20% to 25% of their body weight, depending on the dose. Eli Lilly scientists also contributed to the research as study co-authors.

"Participants had remarkable responses," Schnitzer stated. "Many of the people in this study lost considerable amounts of weight, with a few losing up to a hundred pounds or more.".

Why Diet and Exercise Still Matter.

Despite the encouraging findings, Schnitzer emphasized that lifestyle changes should remain the starting point for people who are overweight and have painful knee osteoarthritis.

Improving eating habits, increasing physical activity, and making other sustainable lifestyle adjustments can help reduce symptoms without the expense of newer weight-loss medications. These strategies also avoid side effects associated with GLP-1 drugs, including gastrointestinal problems and muscle loss.

Recent findings suggest that maintaining muscle strength is particularly important for people with knee osteoarthritis because the muscles surrounding the joint help support and stabilize it. Losing too much muscle could therefore create additional challenges for patients who already have difficulty moving comfortably.

Recent findings suggest that for individuals who cannot achieve sufficient weight loss through lifestyle changes and continue to experience significant knee pain, Schnitzer believes retatrutide could become a valuable option if it receives approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.

Could the Drug Also Slow Knee Arthritis Progression?

Although the trials demonstrated substantial improvements in weight and pain, several important questions remain unanswered.

Industry observers note that one of the biggest is whether retatrutide does more than relieve symptoms. Researchers still do not know if the drug can slow the underlying progression of knee osteoarthritis enough to reduce the likelihood that patients will eventually need knee replacement surgery. People who already required a knee replacement were excluded from the trials.

"That would be the goal here to say you can reduce people's pain, and you can stop the progression of their osteoarthritis," Schnitzer remarked.

Another unanswered question is whether retatrutide might benefit people with painful knee osteoarthritis who are not overweight. Because the trials did not include these patients, further studies will be needed to determine whether they could experience similar improvements.

Researchers are also interested in understanding how much of the pain relief comes directly from weight loss and how much might be related to the drug's effects on inflammation.

In a recent development, "These drugs are believed to have significant anti-inflammatory activity, but the mechanism is not entirely known," Schnitzer said. "Whether cutting down inflammation in the joint is also important in addition to reducing load needs more research, so this is still a first step, in my view. I've been working in the OA field for a long time, and I think this opens up opportunities to do a lot more studies to understand the condition better.".

How Researchers Measured Knee Pain Relief.

To evaluate changes in symptoms, the research teams used the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Arthritis Index (WOMAC) Pain index, a standardized tool for assessing osteoarthritis pain.

During study visits, participants rated their pain on a scale from 0 to 10. They also used a mobile app to record their pain levels each day, allowing researchers to track how symptoms changed throughout treatment.

The study is titled, "Retatrutide Once Weekly in Adults with Knee Osteoarthritis Pain and Obesity.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In their (slightly belated) fresh years message to players, the developer of EA’s The Sims series of games has lightly addressed concerns about its future within the publisher in a wide-ranging letter to the community.

The letter also serves as something of a light plan for what players can expect soon, and in the future, alongside what the various teams are at the moment working on.

The developer starts off the yearly check-in with a statement that attempts to address concerns about the future of The Sims, historically one of EA’s most inclusive and culturally diverse franchises.

It has been revealed that this, of course, comes in the wake of last year’s bombshell that EA is being taken private by a coalition led by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF), alongside investment firms Silver Lake Capital and Affinity Partners. The $55 billion acquisition was approved by EA’s shareholders in December, and is set to close by the end of June.

Understandably, many raised concerns about what EA’s upcoming ownership would mean for its people, and portfolio of games. The news is concerning for The Sims in particular, a series that’s long embraced diversity and inclusivity, and has historically been popular among women, people of colour, and members of the LGBTQ+ community.

“Our Sims team's creative control, guided by our values of inclusivity, choice, creativity, community, and play, has not changed,” the post reads, though without referring to the buyout directly at any point.

“These values inspire the decisions we make each and every day as we initiative for today, tomorrow, and the future.”.

According to recent reports, as for what’s to come in 2026 and beyond, it sounds like The Sims team has multiple irons in the fire. The developer is working on “a family of new Sims experiences” that will find homes on PC, console, and mobile. Crucially, the post indicates that not every experience will be on every platform, in order for each to focus on delivering something different and interesting.

Industry observers note that future releases, of course, include new The Sims 4 content that focuses on the single-player experience. The social and more multiplayer-driven experiences, however, will instead be found in Project Rene, the mobile-first life-sim presently in development. (Despite early confidence that it was a working title for The Sims 5, it's now confirmed that Project Rene won’t, in fact, be a direct successor to The Sims 4.).
